notable.summary: Find an example that is symmetric under time reversal yet not stationary, then prove that time symmetry plus invariance under time shifts implies staticity, and conclude that a stationary time-symmetric system is static.
notable.why_notable: Forces the learner to disentangle three symmetry notions that are easily conflated.

notable.summary: Starting from a block-diagonal time-independent metric, show that the coordinate time vector is a timelike Killing vector orthogonal to the constant-time slices.
notable.why_notable: Completes the converse direction of the static biconditional left unproved in the text.

notable.summary: Compute how far a point on a sphere moves under small increments of each angle and combine the displacements by Pythagoras to obtain the round sphere metric.
notable.why_notable: Gentle entry point for novices; note the misprint in part (ii), which should read phi -> phi + dphi.

notable.summary: Use the contracted Bianchi identities to show that the angular Einstein equation is automatically satisfied once the other three vanish.
notable.why_notable: Shows concretely how the identities reduce the field equations, a theme of Chapter 13.

notable.summary: Determine all non-vanishing components of the covariant Riemann tensor of the Schwarzschild metric.
notable.why_notable: Needed to see that r = 2m is not a curvature singularity and to discuss tidal forces in Chapter 17.

notable.summary: Decide which of the six listed properties of the Schwarzschild exterior remain evident in the isotropic chart.
notable.why_notable: Tests whether learners distinguish chart-dependent features (adaptedness) from geometric ones.

notable.summary: In Cartesian-type isotropic coordinates, verify by direct computation that time translation and the three rotations are Killing vectors and find their commutators.
notable.why_notable: Links the rigorous SO(3) definition of spherical symmetry back to an explicit metric.

notable.summary: Multi-part derivation of the interior theory: fluid tensor components, the mass-function form of lambda, the conservation equation, the TOV equation, and the full uniform-density solution joined to the exterior.
notable.why_notable: Fills in every step the text labels as an exercise in 15.8; a careful solver will also catch the misprint in (15.77).

difficulty.notes: The Schwarzschild derivation itself is routine once Exercise 6.32 is available, but 15.2 relies on fluent index gymnastics (antisymmetrization, dummy index raising, closed-implies-exact) and 15.4 mixes a rigorous definition with a heuristic argument whose hidden assumptions are not stated. Physical interpretation is brief and deferred to Chapters 16-17. The TOV section compresses most steps into exercises. Symbol overloading (lambda, rho, phi) and two printed errors ((15.41) factor, (15.77) interior term) add friction.

teaching_gems.gem: Three-panel pipe picture: changing flow, steady flow, no flow, as the anchor for non-stationary, stationary, static.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Concrete, memorable, and it isolates the key idea that stationarity is about fields at fixed points, not about particles being at rest.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Animated pipe with a 'reverse time' button next to a metric card that gains or loses g_0alpha terms as the mode changes.

teaching_gems.gem: Upgrade a statement made in one convenient chart to a geometric fact: L_X g is a tensor, so showing it is zero in the adapted chart shows it is zero everywhere.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives learners a reusable template for turning 'look how simple the metric is in these coordinates' into geometry.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Show the Schwarzschild metric in a randomly time-mixed chart where every component depends on t'; let the learner compute L_X g numerically along a suggested X and watch it vanish.

teaching_gems.gem: Sign-flip argument: under a reflection only the cross term changes sign, so invariance kills it (used for t, theta and phi).
teaching_gems.why_effective: One short symmetry argument replaces pages of algebra and recurs in many later derivations (Kerr, cosmology).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Metric-matrix widget: learner applies reflections to a generic 4x4 metric and sees which entries flip sign and are forced to zero.

teaching_gems.gem: Coordinate freedom as a budget: areal radius, integrating-factor time and time rescaling each remove one unknown function before physics enters.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes explicit which parts of the final answer are gauge and which are physical, preparing Birkhoff's theorem.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Step-through derivation panel counting remaining free functions (A, B, C, D -> nu, lambda -> m) with each transformation highlighted.

teaching_gems.gem: The time function h(t) that appears in the solution is pure coordinate choice, which is exactly why a spherical vacuum is static (Birkhoff).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners see the theorem emerge from the calculation rather than being asserted.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Let learners choose h(t) (e.g. oscillating) and see a 'time-dependent' metric whose clocks and orbits are identical after relabelling t.

teaching_gems.gem: Fix the integration constant by the weak-field limit, and notice it has units of length.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Connects an abstract constant to a number the learner can compute for the Sun or a neutron star.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Mass-to-length converter with a slider across Earth, Sun, neutron star and M87*, showing m and 2m against the body radius.

teaching_gems.gem: A property checklist for the solution (spherical, stationary, adapted, static, asymptotically flat, geometric mass) re-tested in a new chart.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Distinguishes coordinate-dependent presentation from invariant properties, and gives the tutor an assessment rubric.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Checklist card that toggles between Schwarzschild, isotropic and Eddington-Finkelstein forms, asking the learner which properties are still visible.

teaching_gems.gem: Reuse the vacuum Einstein components with a source: G^0_0 integrates to the mass function and conservation gives the pressure gradient, yielding TOV with little new algebra.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows the economy of the formalism and makes each relativistic correction to Newtonian hydrostatics traceable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: TOV integrator: learner picks an equation of state and central density; plots p(r), m(r), e^nu and compares with the Newtonian profile, flagging the uniform-density 9M/4 limit.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed (15.77) has (1 - 2M/r)^{1/2} in the first term of the interior branch; it must be (1 - 2M/R)^{1/2}.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: With r in place of R the metric is not continuous at the surface and does not satisfy (15.72); learners checking Exercise 15.18(v) will be confused.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use e^nu = [3/2 sqrt(1 - 2M/R) - 1/2 sqrt(1 - 2Mr^2/R^3)]^2 and verify continuity at r = R explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The relation in (15.41) between the two mixed tr components carries e^{lambda - nu}; raising and lowering with diag(e^nu, -e^lambda, ...) gives e^{nu - lambda}.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Harmless for the vacuum solution (only lambda-dot = 0 is used) but misleading for anyone checking index gymnastics.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Derive the ratio directly from G_01 and state it with the correct exponent.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The text calls world-time coordinates Gaussian because g_0a = delta_0a, which requires g_00 = 1; a general static chart has g_0alpha = 0 but g_00 varying.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Encourages the belief that world time is proper time for static observers, blurring the source of gravitational red shift.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say the chart is orthogonal (zero shift) with lapse sqrt(g_00); Gaussian normal coordinates additionally need unit lapse.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The heuristic route to the spherical ansatz silently assumes a central origin, that D(t, r) has a non-vanishing spacelike gradient so sqrt(D) can serve as a radial coordinate, and that A' is non-zero when the integrating-factor step divides by it.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners do not see where the argument could fail: the r < 2m region (areal-radius gradient timelike) and product geometries with constant D, which are excluded for Lambda = 0 vacuum by the field equations but do occur with a cosmological constant or electromagnetic field (Nariai, Bertotti-Robinson). Birkhoff can then be over-applied.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: List the assumptions explicitly, note that constant-D vacuum solutions are ruled out only once G_ab = 0 with Lambda = 0 is imposed, and point to Chapter 17 for the r < 2m region.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Only a partial converse (for Killing vectors) of the hypersurface-orthogonality condition is proved, and Frobenius' theorem is not named.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think the condition is special to Killing fields, missing the link to irrotational flows and later twist of congruences (§23.9).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Mention Frobenius and the fluid-vorticity analogy; show a twisting counterexample.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Asymptotic flatness is said to be forced, but this depends on zero cosmological constant; with Lambda the unique spherical vacuum is Schwarzschild-de Sitter.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Overgeneralisation when learners meet cosmology (Chapters 24-26) or the cosmological term of §13.3.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a one-line caveat and optionally show the -Lambda r^2/3 term appearing in e^{-lambda}.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The interior section omits the Buchdahl compactness limit implied by (15.76), and does not discuss the difference between m(r) and proper-volume mass.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Misses the most striking physical consequence of TOV (stars cannot be arbitrarily compact) and the idea that binding energy counts toward gravitating mass.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Evaluate p(0), find R = 9M/4, and compare 4 pi r^2 dr with the proper volume element e^{lambda/2} 4 pi r^2 dr.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Symbol overloading: lambda (three meanings), rho (radius and density), phi (angle and potential), prime (derivative and new coordinate).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion when reading 15.2, 15.4, 15.7 and 15.8 in sequence.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: In the app use distinct symbols (e.g. alpha for the proportionality factor, Omega for the conformal factor, bar r for isotropic radius).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Birkhoff's theorem is contrasted with Newtonian theory as 'unexpected', yet Newtonian gravity also has a time-independent exterior potential for spherical pulsations (shell theorem).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: May attribute to non-linearity something that is shared with linear theories; the real novelty is that the entire exterior geometry is static and unique.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present Newtonian and Maxwell analogues, then emphasise what is new in GR (static metric, no monopole waves, uniqueness of geometry).

tutor_notes: Open with: 'A river flows steadily past you; is the river static?' Use the answer to separate stationary (steady) from static (no flow), then ask for an astrophysical example of each (rotating star versus non-rotating star).
Before any index work, check the learner can explain why a metric that looks time-dependent in one chart might still be stationary; if not, show a time-mixed coordinate change of Minkowski space.

Order for a first pass: pipe picture -> Killing vector definition of stationary -> reflection argument for static -> spherical ansatz -> solve for Schwarzschild -> Birkhoff and m = GM/c^2. Postpone the hypersurface-orthogonality proof (15.2) to a second pass or for mathematically oriented learners.
When presenting hypersurface orthogonality, use the level sets of t in Schwarzschild as the concrete example first: X_a = (1 - 2m/r) partial_a t is visibly a multiple of a gradient.
Check for understanding: ask which of the coordinate transformations in 15.4-15.5 changed the physics (none) and which constant survives as physical (m).
Common question: 'Is r the distance from the centre?' Answer that r is defined by sphere area; proper radial distance differs, and isotropic rho is yet another label for the same spheres.

Common question: 'Does Birkhoff mean a collapsing star has no effect outside?' Yes for the geometry outside the star's surface as long as the collapse stays spherical and the mass is conserved; ripples need asymmetry.
Use numbers: have the learner compute m for the Earth (about 4.4 mm) and the Sun (about 1.5 km) to feel how weak ordinary fields are (2m/R ~ 1e-9 and 4e-6).
Warn about printed slips: (15.77) should contain 2M/R in the constant term, and the exponent in (15.41) should be nu - lambda. Encourage learners to verify continuity at r = R themselves.

For TOV, ask the learner to take the Newtonian limit term by term (p << rho, 4 pi r^3 p << m, 2m/r << 1) and name what each relativistic factor means: pressure has inertia, pressure gravitates, and space is stretched.
Stretch question for advanced learners: evaluate the central pressure of the uniform-density star and find the radius where it diverges (R = 9M/4).
Signature reminder: this book uses (+,-,-,-); when learners bring formulas from Carroll or Schutz, flip the sign of g_ab and of p g^ab terms accordingly.
If a learner asks why a Killing vector is needed rather than just 'no t in the metric', point to the Kerr metric (Chapter 20): stationary with cross terms that no chart can remove, hence not static.
